title: The Dinosaur-Killing Rock Was a Rare Space Visitor!
summary:
What if I told you the giant rock that killed the dinosaurs was a super rare space traveler? Scientists just figured out exactly what kind of meteorite slammed into Earth 66 million years ago and caused the extinction of almost all dinosaurs. It was a type called a CO chondrite—and it's not like the meteorites you see in museums!

So what's a CO chondrite? It's a very old, primitive space rock that formed when our solar system was just a baby. It has less sulfur, carbon, and water than other meteorites. That's a big clue because scientists used to think the sulfur from the impactor helped block the sun and freeze the planet. But this new finding suggests that the real killer was the enormous cloud of fine dust and debris that got blasted into the sky.

How did they solve this mystery? The meteorite itself vaporized when it hit, leaving behind a thin layer of clay all over the Earth. Scientists from Canada, France, Belgium, and Austria collected samples of that clay and measured its nickel isotopes—like a chemical fingerprint. The fingerprint matched CO chondrites, which make up only a tiny fraction of all meteorites found on Earth.

The dinosaur-killing rock was huge—about 6 miles wide—and hit at 64,000 kilometers per hour, creating the Chicxulub crater under Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Dr. Philippe Claeys, one of the researchers, said, 'Being impacted by such a rare, distant projectile really underscores how unlucky the dinosaurs were.' So next time you see a shooting star, remember: some space rocks are way more special than others!
why_it_matters: Understanding the space rock that ended the dinosaurs helps us learn about Earth's history and how to protect our planet in the future.

background_read: The dinosaur extinction is known as the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) event, and it wiped out roughly 75% of all species.
Scientists previously discovered a worldwide layer of the rare metal iridium, which first suggested that a giant meteorite was the cause.
The Chicxulub crater, buried under Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, is the scar left by that colossal impact.
Article_Structure: WHO: The giant meteorite and researchers like Dr. Philippe Claeys.
WHAT: A rare CO chondrite space rock hit Earth, wiping out dinosaurs.
WHERE: Impacted near Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, leaving the Chicxulub crater.
WHY: To learn what kind of rock caused the extinction and how it happened.

perspectives.description: Identifying the meteorite as a rare CO chondrite gives scientists a clearer picture of the event that shaped life on Earth.
The impact wiped out entire groups of animals, showing how a single cosmic event can change the planet forever.
The study uses advanced chemical fingerprints to solve a 66-million-year-old puzzle.
